stages.title: Advanced Hebrew Literature
stages.statusNote: Dead Sea Scrolls Hebrew, Mishnaic Hebrew, medieval commentary and later theological Hebrew are a later expansion. Each needs its own texts, lexicon and grammar: Biblical Hebrew morphology does not suffice for them, and the library holds none of them in analysed form. The course does not claim to teach them.

objectives.can: Name each of the twenty-two consonants, give its sound, and read from right to left.
Recognise the five final forms and tell apart the letters that look alike.
Name the full vowel points and read a consonant with its vowel.
Tell a vocal shewa from a silent one and recognise the three composite shewas.
Tell dagesh lene from dagesh forte, read the six begadkefat letters, and say how the gutturals behave.
Read ה, ו and י as vowel letters where they are, divide a word into syllables and find its stress.
Read words joined by maqqef as one unit, recognise sof pasuq, atnah and silluq, and read a whole verse aloud.
Give the gender and number of a noun, including the dual.
Recognise ten of the commonest nouns of the Hebrew Bible.
Separate a prefixed article, preposition or conjunction from its word and name it.
Recognise ten more common nouns.
Match an adjective or demonstrative to its noun, and tell the attributive from the predicate use.
Recognise a noun in the construct state and read a construct chain as 'X of Y'.
Recognise ten more common nouns, with their construct forms.
Identify the pronominal suffix on a noun: its person, gender and number.
Recognise the independent personal pronouns and their person, gender and number.
Read the common prepositions with and without suffixes, and recognise אֵת marking a definite object.
Recognise the commonest prepositions and particles.
Read a clause with no verb, finding its subject and predicate, and the Hebrew ways of saying 'have'.
Recognise a Qal qatal form and give its person, gender and number.
Recognise ten of the commonest verbs.
Recognise a Qal yiqtol form and give its person, gender and number.
Recognise Qal imperatives and their gender and number.
Read לֹא, אַל and אֵין and say what kind of sentence each negates.
Tell the infinitive construct from the infinitive absolute and name the commonest use of each.
Recognise the Qal active and passive participles and parse their gender, number and state.
Find the verb, subject and object of a verbal clause and notice when something stands before the verb.
Recognise a wayyiqtol form, parse it, and read it as the next event of a narrative.
Recognise weqatal and read it as continuing a future, a command or a habitual action.
Tell the main line of a narrative from its background: wayyiqtol chains broken by וְ + subject + qatal, participles and verbless clauses; and read וַיְהִי with a time expression.
Mark where speech begins and ends, and notice the change of verb forms inside it.
Read a clause with אֲשֶׁר, find what it refers to, and choose the right sense of כִּי.
Read Ruth 1 through, following the wayyiqtol chain and the speeches, with help only where asked.
Name the stem of a verb form from its marks: prefixed נ or ה, a doubled middle consonant, prefixed הִתְ.
Recognise and parse Niphal forms and say how the verb's Niphal is related to its Qal.
Recognise and parse Piel and Pual forms.
Recognise and parse Hiphil and Hophal forms.
Recognise and parse Hithpael forms, including those where the ת changes place.
Recognise the rarer stems when met, and compare the forms and senses of one root in several stems.
Parse verbs with a guttural as first, second or third root consonant and explain their changed vowels.
Recognise forms where a first נ has assimilated or dropped, and restore the root.
Recognise forms of roots beginning with י, and of הָלַךְ, and restore the root.
Recognise forms of roots with ו or י in the middle and restore the root.
Recognise forms of roots ending in ה, including the shortened forms of the jussive and wayyiqtol.
Recognise forms of roots whose second and third consonants are alike, and of doubly weak verbs.
Recognise the cohortative and the jussive and read them as wish, command or resolve.
Parse the common irregular nouns in their construct, plural and suffixed forms.
Identify a pronominal object suffix on a verb.
Classify a clause as verbal, nominal or participial, and say what הִנֵּה, עַתָּה, גַּם, אַךְ, רַק, לָכֵן and עַל־כֵּן signal.
Recognise a condition with אִם, כִּי, לוּ or no particle at all, and say what it supposes.
Recognise purpose and result expressed by לְ with the infinitive, לְמַעַן, בַּעֲבוּר, פֶּן, and by a volitive form after another.
Read an infinitive construct with its subject and object, an infinitive absolute, and a participle as predicate, attribute or noun.
Notice a constituent placed before the verb or detached at the head of a clause, and consider what it marks.
Describe what qatal, yiqtol, wayyiqtol, weqatal and the participle each tend to do in narrative, in speech and in poetry, and state the main points on which scholars disagree.
Divide a verse of poetry into its lines and describe how the second line answers the first.
Read poetic lines that omit a verb, the article, אֵת or אֲשֶׁר, and recognise poetic forms and word order.
concepts: qatal and yiqtol in parallel lines

objectives.can: Read a short psalm, recognising its common vocabulary and its movement from address to petition to praise.
Recognise twelve words characteristic of the Psalms.
Read two-line proverbs and a passage of Job, coping with rare words by their parallel.
Read a prophetic oracle: messenger formula, direct address, word-play and imagery; and use the accents as a record of how the tradition phrased the verse.
Read a narrative chapter of Genesis with reduced help.
Read the prose of Samuel: longer scenes, quick dialogue and some hard text.
Read Jonah 1 continuously with only occasional help.
Read a longer psalm independently, line by line.
Read a chapter of Isaiah, handling its poetry, rare words and long sentences.

authoring.by: Written for Ecclesia by Claude (Anthropic), following the public-domain grammars listed as sources. Every Hebrew word shown as an example, in a paradigm or in an exercise is taken from the Westminster Leningrad Codex as analysed by the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project.
